title: A word of wisdom on food and drink carries a promise
setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation in Kirtland, Ohio, on 27 February 1833. No record from the time describes the occasion. Later accounts tie it to the school of the prophets, which met at Newel K. Whitney’s store. Brigham Young, who was not present, later said tobacco use there troubled Emma Smith and others, so Joseph asked the Lord. Temperance societies were active across America and in Kirtland at the time.
summary: The opening verses address the high priests in Kirtland, the church, and the Saints in Zion. They call the revelation a word of wisdom, given “not by commandment or constraint”. The voice says it warns against the designs of “conspiring men” in the last days. Wine and strong drink are not good, except homemade grape wine for the sacrament. Strong drink is for washing the body, and tobacco is for bruises and sick cattle; “hot drinks” are not for the body. Herbs, fruit, and grain are ordained for human use, and meat is to be used sparingly. Those who keep these sayings and obey are promised health, wisdom, and strength to run without weariness. The destroying angel will pass them by, as it passed ancient Israel.

contextNote.title: A principle fitted to the weakest Saint
contextNote.text: Verse 2 says the revelation came “not by commandment or constraint”. So why would members keep it? Verse 3 answers by calling it “a principle with promise”. It is also fitted to “the weakest of all saints,” so no one is beyond its reach. Verses 18–21 spell out the promise: health, hidden knowledge, endurance, and protection. The promise depends on keeping these sayings while “walking in obedience to the commandments”. Here, a principle with promise is counsel that carries its own reward for those who follow it.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 89–92, “A Principle with Promise,” presents the Word of Wisdom as care for both body and spirit. Which promises in verses 18–21 reach beyond physical health?
reviewNote: Read all 21 verses. Official heading gives Kirtland, 27 February 1833, and tobacco use in meetings troubling Emma Smith. JSP introduction read: no contemporary account of the dictation; later recollections (Brigham Young secondhand, Zebedee Coltrin) tie it to the school of the prophets in Whitney’s store; Kirtland Temperance Society context; uneven early observance. Independence included for “the saints in Zion” in verse 1.
